blocks.content: What does it intuitively mean to assert that `f(n) ∈ O(g(n))`?
That `g(n)` works as an asymptotic upper bound for `f(n)`, except for constants and from a certain input size.
Correct. Big-O describes maximum asymptotic growth: `f(n)` does not grow faster than `g(n)` except for constant factors.
That `f(n)` and `g(n)` always have exactly the same value for all `n`.
Wrong. Big-O notation does not require exact equality of values; compares asymptotic growth.
That `f(n)` is always larger than `g(n)` for small inputs.
Wrong. Big-O is not decided by small inputs, but by behavior from some `n0` onwards.
That `f(n)` is necessarily the best possible bound for `g(n)`.
Incorrect. Big-O only indicates an upper bound; It does not guarantee that it is tight.
`f(n) ∈ O(g(n))` means that there exists a constant `c > 0` and a point `n0` from which `f(n) ≤ c·g(n)`. It is an asymptotic upper bound.
What does it intuitively mean to assert that `f(n) ∈ Ω(g(n))`?
That `g(n)` works as an asymptotic lower bound for `f(n)`, except for constants and from a certain input size.
Correct. Big-Ω indicates that `f(n)` grows at least as fast as `g(n)`, up to constants.
That `f(n)` is superiorly bounded by `g(n)`.
Wrong. That's Big-O's idea, not Big-Ω's.
That `f(n)` and `g(n)` are exactly the same for all `n`.
Wrong. Big-Ω compares asymptotic growth, not exact equality.
That `g(n)` always dominates `f(n)` in growth.
Wrong. If `f(n) ∈ Ω(g(n))`, then `f(n)` does not fall below `g(n)` asymptotically, except constants.
`f(n) ∈ Ω(g(n))` means that, from a certain point, `f(n)` is at least a positive constant multiplied by `g(n)`. It is an asymptotic lower bound.
What does it intuitively mean to assert that `f(n) ∈ Θ(g(n))`?
That `f(n)` and `g(n)` have the same order of asymptotic growth, except for multiplicative constants.
Correct. Big-Θ indicates upper and lower bound simultaneously.
That `f(n)` is less than `g(n)` only for small values of `n`.
Wrong. Big-Θ is not defined by small values, but by asymptotic growth.
That `f(n)` is only an upper bound of `g(n)`.
Wrong. Big-Θ requires two directions: adjusted upper and lower bounds.
That `f(n)` is always worth zero when `g(n)` increases.
Wrong. That statement does not describe asymptotic equivalence.
`Θ(g(n))` describes a tight bound: `f(n)` does not grow either asymptotically faster or asymptotically slower than `g(n)`, except for constants.
What is the difference between an upper bound and an adjusted bound?
An upper bound only limits above; A tight dimension limits above and below with the same order.
Correct. `O(g(n))` may be an unadjusted upper bound; `Θ(g(n))` indicates adjusted growth.
An upper limit is always more accurate than an adjusted limit.
Wrong. The fitted bound is usually more informative because it describes the actual order of growth.
A fitted dimension is only used for constant functions.
Wrong. Fitted bounds are used for constant, logarithmic, polynomial, exponential, and many more functions.
There is no difference; both mean exact equality.
Wrong. None demands exact equality; compare asymptotic growth.
An upper bound may be true but weak. For example, `n ∈ O(n²)` is true, but `n ∈ Θ(n)` is more precise.
If `f(n)=3n²+10n+7`, why does `Θ(n²)` describe your growth better than `O(n³)`?
Because `n²` is the true dominant term, while `O(n³)` is a true but looser upper bound.
Correct. `Θ(n²)` captures the adjusted order of the function.
Because `O(n³)` is always false for any quadratic function.
Wrong. A quadratic function does belong to `O(n³)`, but that bound is not adjusted.
Because the term `10n` dominates `3n²`.
Wrong. For large values, `n²` dominates `n`.
Because constants do not exist in algorithm analysis.
Wrong. Constants exist and affect real time; What happens is that they do not change the dominant asymptotic class.
Although `O(n³)` is a valid upper bound, it does not describe adjusted growth. The dominant term of `3n²+10n+7` is `n²`, so the adjusted class is `Θ(n²)`.
Why say that `3n+5 ∈ O(n²)` may be true but uninformative?
Because `n²` does limit `3n+5` superiorly, but it does not describe its adjusted growth.
Correct. The statement is valid, but a more accurate description would be `Θ(n)`.
Because `3n+5` cannot be compared with `n²`.
Wrong. Yes they can be compared; in fact `n²` is an upper bound, although not adjusted.
Because Big-O must always use exactly the same complete original function.
Wrong. The asymptotic notation just allows us to simplify to a representative growth function.
Because any linear function is outside Big-O.
Wrong. Linear functions can be in Big-O of many functions that limit them superiorly.
`O(n²)` is true for `3n+5`, but it hides that the function actually grows linearly. An adjusted bound would be `Θ(n)`.
Order the following functions from lowest to highest asymptotic growth.
`log n`
`log n` grows slower than any positive power of `n`.
`n` grows faster than `log n`, but slower than `n log n`.
`n log n`
`n log n` is between linear and quadratic growth.
`n²`
`n²` dominates `n log n`, but is below exponential functions.
`2^n` dominates any polynomial of fixed degree, but is dominated by `n!`.
`n!` grows faster than `2^n` for large values of `n`.
The correct order is `log n`, `n`, `n log n`, `n²`, `2^n`, `n!`. This hierarchy is a basis for comparing algorithmic costs.
Compare `n²` and `n log n`: which dominates asymptotically?
`n²` dominates `n log n`.
Correct. After dividing by `n`, it remains to compare `n` with `log n`; `n` dominates.
`n log n` dominates `n²` because it has a logarithm.
Wrong. The additional `n` factor in `n²` dominates the `log n` factor.
Both functions belong to `Θ(n)`.
Wrong. Neither of them is linear tight.
They cannot be compared because one has a logarithm and the other does not.
Wrong. Yes, they can be compared using quotients, limits or growth hierarchies.
The ratio `n²/(n log n)=n/log n` tends to infinity. That's why `n²` grows faster than `n log n`.
Compare `2^n` and `n^5`: which dominates asymptotically?
`2^n` dominates `n^5`.
Correct. Any exponential with a base greater than 1 dominates any polynomial of fixed degree.
`n^5` dominates `2^n` because it has exponent 5.
Wrong. In `n^5` the exponent is constant; in `2^n` the variable is in the exponent.
Both functions are `Θ(n^5)`.
Wrong. An exponential is not in the same adjusted class as a polynomial of fixed degree.
It depends on the machine where the algorithm is run.
Wrong. The asymptotic comparison between functions is not machine dependent.
Exponentials with a constant base greater than 1 grow faster than any polynomial of constant degree. Therefore, `2^n` dominates `n^5`.
`log(n³)` and `log n` belong to the same class `Θ`.
True
Correct. `log(n³)=3 log n`, and the constant factor 3 does not change the `Θ` class.
False
Wrong. The power within the logarithm is transformed into a constant factor: `log(n³)=3 log n`.
By properties of logarithms, `log(n³)=3log(n)`. Since Big-Θ ignores positive multiplicative constants, both functions are `Θ(log n)`.
Compare `5n³ + n` and `n³ - 100n²`. Which term asymptotically dominates in both functions?
In both the cubic term `n³` dominates.
Correct. The lower degree terms become negligible compared to `n³` for large values ​​of `n`.
In the first `n` dominates, and in the second `-100n²` dominates.
Wrong. Terms of lower degree do not dominate the cubic term asymptotically.
In both, the term invisible constant dominates.
Wrong. There is no dominant constant term, and even if it existed, it would not dominate a cubic.
You cannot know why a function has a subtraction.
Wrong. The presence of a subtraction does not prevent the identification of the dominant term for large values.
Both functions have a cubic dominant term. Therefore, both belong to `Θ(n³)` under standard asymptotic analysis.
If `lim f(n)/g(n) = c` with `0 < c < ∞`, what asymptotic relationship exists between `f` and `g`?
Correct. A positive and finite limit indicates that both functions grow at the same order.
Wrong. For `o(g(n))`, the quotient `f(n)/g(n)` should tend to 0.
`f(n)` strictly dominates `g(n)`.
Wrong. If the quotient tends to a positive constant, neither strictly dominates the other.
Nothing can be concluded about growth.
Wrong. That limit is a direct tool to conclude order equivalence.
If the quotient between two functions tends to a positive and finite constant, their growths are equivalent in `Θ` notation.
If `lim f(n)/g(n) = 0`, what can be concluded about `f` relative to `g`, using the `f/g` quotient convention?
`f(n)` grows strictly slower than `g(n)` in the asymptotic sense.
Correct. If `f/g` tends to 0, then `f` is asymptotically below `g`.
`f(n)` and `g(n)` have exactly the same adjusted growth.
Wrong. For adjusted growth the ratio should tend to a positive and finite constant.
`f(n)` dominates `g(n)`.
Wrong. It's the opposite: `g(n)` dominates `f(n)` with this convention.
The limit is not useful for comparing functions.
Incorrect. Ratio limits are a standard tool for comparing growth.
With the `f/g` convention, if the limit is 0, `f` is asymptotically less than `g`; informally, `g` dominates `f`.
If `lim f(n)/g(n) = ∞`, what can be concluded about `f` relative to `g`, using the `f/g` quotient convention?
`f(n)` grows strictly faster than `g(n)` in the asymptotic sense.
Correct. If `f/g` tends to infinity, `f` dominates `g`.
`f(n)` grows strictly slower than `g(n)`.
Wrong. That would happen if `f/g` tended to 0.
`f(n)` and `g(n)` are equivalent in `Θ`.
Wrong. For `Θ` equivalence, the quotient should tend to a positive and finite constant.
The comparison is impossible because infinity cannot appear in limits.
Wrong. That a limit diverges to infinity is a valid conclusion in comparison of growth.
With the `f/g` convention, an infinite limit indicates that `f` grows faster than `g`.
Why is it dangerous to mix the `lim f(n)/g(n)` and `lim g(n)/f(n)` conventions without clarifying which one is being used?
Because reversing the quotient reverses the interpretation of who dominates who.

Because both quotients always produce the same limit.
Wrong. If one tends to 0, the other tends to infinity, when the functions are positive.
Because limits cannot be used in asymptotic notation.
Wrong. Limits are useful; The problem is changing the convention without warning.
Because Big-O only allows comparing constant functions.
Wrong. Big-O compares many classes of functions, not just constants.
The conclusion depends on which function is above in the quotient. Using `f/g` or `g/f` without clarifying it can completely change the reading of a 0 or infinite limit.

What is the difference between `o(g(n))` and `O(g(n))`?

Correct. Little-o is a strict upper bound; Big-O is an upper bound that is not necessarily strict.
`o(g(n))` and `O(g(n))` mean exactly the same thing.
Wrong. Little-o is stronger: excludes the tight same-order case.
`O(g(n))` requires strictly lower growth than `g(n)`.
Wrong. Big-O allows `f` to have the same order as `g`.
`o(g(n))` is only used for constant functions.
Wrong. Little-o can be used with logarithmic, polynomial, exponential and many other functions.

What is the difference between `ω(g(n))` and `Ω(g(n))`?
`ω(g(n))` requires growth strictly greater than `g(n)`, while `Ω(g(n))` allows growth of greater or the same order.
Correct. Little-omega is a strict lower bound; Big-Ω is not necessarily strict.
`Ω(g(n))` requires strictly higher growth than `g(n)`.
Wrong. Big-Ω allows functions to have the same order.
`ω(g(n))` and `Ω(g(n))` are identical.
Wrong. Little-omega excludes the case of tight same order; Big-Ω does not exclude it.
`ω(g(n))` means that `f(n)` becomes zero.
Wrong. `ω(g(n))` indicates strictly increased growth, not disappearance.
If `f(n) ∈ ω(g(n))`, then `f(n)/g(n) → ∞`. In `Ω(g(n))`, it is enough for `f(n)` to be at least proportional to `g(n)` from a certain point.
What does `f(n) ~ g(n)` mean?
That `lim f(n)/g(n) = 1`, that is, both functions are asymptotically equivalent with reason tending to 1.
Correct. The asymptotic equivalence `~` is stronger than belonging to the same class `Θ`.
That `f(n)` is any upper bound of `g(n)`.
Wrong. That looks like Big-O; `~` requires reason tending to 1.
That `f(n)` grows strictly slower than `g(n)`.
Wrong. If `f ~ g`, none grow strictly slower; They are equivalent in asymptotic ratio.
That `f(n)` and `g(n)` have the same value for all `n`.
Wrong. `~` does not require exact equality for all `n`, but rather equivalence in the limit.
`f(n) ~ g(n)` means that the quotient `f(n)/g(n)` tends to 1. This is why it is a more precise equivalence than `Θ`.
If `f(n) ~ g(n)`, then `f(n) ∈ Θ(g(n))` also holds.
True
Correct. If the quotient tends to 1, then it is also bounded by positive constants.
False
Wrong. The `~` equivalence implies `Θ`, although `Θ` does not necessarily imply `~`.
If `f(n)/g(n) → 1`, then for large values the quotient is between two positive constants. That meets the definition of `Θ(g(n))`.

You are forgetting that `1000n` is quadratic.

You are using Big-Theta, which does not exist for polynomials.

Because constants are never executed in a real program.

Wrong. In real measurements, the constants can be very visible.
Because constants turn any algorithm into `Θ(1)`.
